prompt.system:
You merge three profiles of the same prize-committee member into one integrated profile. Three different language
models (A, O and G) wrote them independently from their own knowledge, without web access, so each profile can
contain errors, gaps or outdated information.

- Use only what the three profiles say. Do not add facts, works, years, coauthors or roles from your own knowledge.
- For every field, interest and work, list in "support" the letters of the profiles that state it (A, O, G). Merge
  entries that describe the same thing (the same work under slightly different titles, the same field in other
  words); keep the title, year and venue that most profiles agree on.
- Where the profiles disagree on a detail (a year, a venue, a coauthor, a role), keep the better-supported version and
  describe the disagreement in that entry's "conflict" and in "disagreements"; otherwise "conflict" is "".
- Keep entries that only one profile states, with that single letter. Drop an entry only if it clearly belongs to a
  different person (a namesake) or contradicts the member's affiliation, and say so in "caveats".
- Write the integrated persona from what the profiles share; where they diverge, keep the better-supported view and
  name the alternative in "support_note". Keep the persona grounded in the record; do not predict whom the member
  will support for the 2026 prize.
- "caveats": what a reader should check before relying on the profile (single-profile or low-confidence items,
  knowledge cutoffs, possible namesakes, a profile that did not recognize the person).

persona.summary: A Stockholm-based quantitative macroeconomist and public economist whose work spans dynamic political economy of the welfare state and climate-economy integrated assessment. As 2026 chair, the profiles expect him to keep deliberation focused on a clearly delineated core contribution, its rigor and robustness, and its durable influence on the discipline.
persona.research_lens: Dynamic general equilibrium: intertemporal tradeoffs, externalities, taxation, technical change, incentives, and the political feasibility and welfare consequences of policy. He asks how tractable theory maps into quantitative policy conclusions and how an idea changes the way economists model behavior, markets and long-run outcomes. He prefers this to judging only whether a result is striking. Per the profiles, this is inferred from his research record.
persona.methods_and_evidence: Formal analytical dynamic models with closed-form insights; dynamic optimization and programming; calibrated quantitative macro models and integrated assessment models; policy counterfactuals; and estimation of key macro elasticities such as energy substitution. He is not anti-empirical, but relies less on micro-econometric design. In deliberation he would likely test whether evidence is disciplined by a coherent mechanism and survives general-equilibrium feedbacks.
persona.what_they_value_in_contributions: Simple, general and tractable results that change policy design (for example, carbon-tax formulas). He values frameworks that become workhorses for later research, methodological rigor combined with policy relevance, and clarity about tradeoffs under uncertainty and over long horizons. He also values bringing macroeconomic tools into new areas such as the environment and political economy, and a clearly attributable core contribution with lasting cross-field influence.

representative_works.title: Optimal Taxes on Fossil Fuel in General Equilibrium
representative_works.contribution: Builds a tractable dynamic (stochastic) general-equilibrium climate-economy model. It derives a simple closed-form optimal carbon tax, proportional to output and depending on discounting, damage elasticity and carbon depreciation.

representative_works.title: Environmental Macroeconomics
representative_works.contribution: Comprehensive survey and framework chapter integrating climate (carbon cycle, damages, energy and policy) into macroeconomic models.
representative_works.conflict: A and G list the coauthors as Per Krusell and Anthony A. Smith Jr.; O lists Per Krusell and Conny Olovsson. The A/G version is kept. Only A specifies Vol. 2.

representative_works.title: Directed Technical Change as a Response to Natural Resource Scarcity
representative_works.contribution: Estimates energy–capital/labor complementarity and models endogenous energy-saving technical change. It explains long-run energy-share patterns and draws out implications for climate policy.

representative_works.title: The Survival of the Welfare State
representative_works.contribution: Dynamic political-economy model in which redistribution shapes future political support through investment incentives. It yields multiple steady states and explains welfare-state persistence or collapse.

representative_works.title: Intelligence, Social Mobility, and Growth
representative_works.contribution: Links ability, social mobility and the allocation of talent to growth, contrasting returns to innate ability with inherited advantage.

representative_works.title: A Positive Theory of Geographic Mobility and Social Insurance
representative_works.contribution: Shows how unemployment insurance and geographic mobility jointly determine political equilibria, helping explain persistent differences between Europe and the US.

representative_works.title: Economics and Climate Change: Integrated Assessment in a Multi-Region World
representative_works.venue: Journal of the European Economic Association
representative_works.contribution: Multi-region integrated assessment model of the distributional effects of climate change and of alternative carbon-tax designs across regions and oil producers.

representative_works.title: Equilibrium Unemployment Insurance
representative_works.contribution: Political-economy / dynamic-equilibrium account of unemployment insurance as an endogenous institution.

A.identity_note: John Hassler, Professor of Economics at the IIES, Stockholm University. He is a macroeconomist known for climate and environmental macroeconomics, much of it with Per Krusell and Conny Olovsson, and for earlier political-economy work on the welfare state and social insurance. He is a long-standing member of the Economics Prize Committee and, to my knowledge, chaired it in 2025, the year of the prize to Mokyr, Aghion and Howitt. He also served on the Swedish Fiscal Policy Council.
A.knowledge_limits: My knowledge runs to roughly 2024–early 2025. I am unsure of his exact committee tenure dates, of his work after 2023, and of exact titles and venues for some of his climate-policy papers. The committee deliberations themselves are confidential, and this persona's views are inferences from his published research, not stated preferences.

O.persona_summary: Hassler would bring the perspective of a quantitative macroeconomist and public economist who has worked both on abstract dynamic models and on highly policy-relevant climate economics. As 2026 chair, he would likely emphasize clarity about the scientific contribution, its durability, and its influence on economics as a discipline, while keeping the discussion anchored in the Nobel committee’s standard of a major, well-established contribution.
O.identity_note: John Hassler is the Stockholm University IIES professor of economics known for macroeconomics, public finance/political economy, and climate-economy macroeconomics. The affiliation in the prompt identifies him unambiguously.
